title: The fourth: peaceful, kind, not two
hookLine: the Mandukya reaches a fourth quarter and lists what it isn't
carry: turiya: the self beneath waking, dream and sleep
tomorrow: a fever shrinks the world to one aching body. does it have to?

cards: A form asks you to tick one box: awake, dreaming, or asleep. The Mandukya has named those three quarters of this self, one after another, each with a name and a job. Then it reaches a fourth, and there's no box for it.
Instead of saying what the fourth is, the text starts listing what it isn't.

teach.h: NOT INWARD, NOT OUTWARD, NOT BOTH.
teach.b: In paraphrase: not knowing inward, not knowing outward, not both. Not a mass of knowing. Unseen, ungraspable, unthinkable, unnameable.
The first nots each rule out a quarter by name: outward was waking, inward was dreaming, a mass of knowing was deep sleep.
So the fourth can't be filed as one more state beside them. Then the tone turns warm. In it, the world comes to rest.
Peaceful, kind, not two. That is the self. That is to be known.
Gaudapada's verses on the Mandukya call it turiya, the fourth. Advaita teachers say it isn't a state you visit. It's the self that waking, dream and sleep all appear in.
No wonder that in the Muktika Upanishad, Rama tells Hanuman the Mandukya alone is enough for a seeker.
Now the week, in one breath. This is that Devadatta, the labels set aside. The inner controller, unknown to the earth it lives in.
Atat, not that: a real difference, and love across it. Ayam: this self, right here. As the desire, so the resolve, so the deed.
Deep sleep, gathered, beside a psalm's peace.
And the fourth, after all the nots: peaceful, kind, not two.

how: In Advaita study, Mandukya 7 is read with Gaudapada's verses, which call the fourth turiya; teachers present it not as a fourth state but as the self that waking, dream and deep sleep appear in.

o: that god is far off, beyond every heaven
this body alone is the whole of who you are
this self, in all its quarters, is Brahman

games.q: the week's readings. tap the pairs.

s: the fourth quarter is described only by what it isn't
after the nots, the text turns warm: peaceful, kind, not two. that is the self, to be known.
Devadatta is a stock name in old Sanskrit examples
a bit like John Doe: this is that Devadatta, older now and the same.

games.q: a friend says the fourth must just be a fourth state, like an extra-deep sleep. what does the Mandukya say?
o: it rules out waking, dream and deep sleep by name: not one more state.
yes: the fourth is the deepest kind of sleep there is.
the fourth is a dream that comes after deep sleep ends.
games.why: not knowing inward, not outward, not a mass of knowing: each quarter ruled out. then: peaceful, kind, not two. that is the self.

practice: Listen for one sound around you, a hum, a car, your own breath, and let it come and go. Between one sound and the next, notice the plain quiet that's there. Rest in it without giving it a name.

wordCard.voice: Ayam atma brahma: this self, and in the Mandukya its fourth quarter, peaceful, kind, not two. The week's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit: turiya, the fourth, the name Gaudapada's verses give the fourth quarter.

carryVoice: For keeps: turiya, the self beneath waking, dream and sleep. Peaceful, kind, not two. A week of sayings, closed.

sources.ref: Mandukya Upanishad 7 (not inwardly knowing, not outwardly knowing, not both, not a mass of knowing, not knowing, not unknowing; unseen, beyond dealings, ungraspable, without marks, unthinkable, unnameable; essence the certainty of the one self; the world comes to rest; peaceful, auspicious, not two; that is thought of as the fourth; that is the self; that is to be known)
Mandukya Upanishad 3–5 (waking knows outward; dream knows inward; deep sleep a mass of knowing)
Gaudapada, Mandukya Karika 1.10–1.16 (the fourth called turiya) — general
Muktika Upanishad 1.26 (Rama tells Hanuman the Mandukya alone is enough for liberation) — general
Vedantasara (this is that Devadatta); Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 3.7 and 4.4.5; Madhva on Chandogya 6.8.7; Mandukya Upanishad 2; Psalm 4:8 (the week's look-back)
Chandogya Upanishad 6.1.4 (by one lump of clay all that is made of clay is known; the change is a name, the clay is real)
